# FP8 KV and decode DeepGEMM losses

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Do FP8 KV storage or DeepGEMM decode improve the routed service without violating both latency limits?

## Why investigate this?

After routing improved the service, two plausible decode-side changes were tested separately: reducing KV representation precision and changing the decode matrix-kernel backend. KV cache stores attention state needed for future tokens; lower precision can reduce its footprint but may affect latency or quality. DeepGEMM is an existing optimized kernel library, not a team-created method. These are candidate mechanisms, not assumed wins.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| KV cache precision | BF16 KV. | FP8 KV tested on the routed pipeline at N52. |
| Decode kernel backend | Existing decode backend. | DeepGEMM decode tested separately at matched N52. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 matched-load tests | Both tested branches failed the joint SLA at N52. |

## What did we learn?

- Neither candidate met the service gate in these tests.
- A decode-only failure does not rule out using DeepGEMM in prefill, whose parallel workload differs.

## Decision

Retain BF16 KV and close these tested branches; later test phase-specific ideas only with their own controls.

## Limits and remaining questions

- The result applies to these implementations, routing, and N52 setup.
- No claim about all FP8 KV or all DeepGEMM versions.

## Sources

- [journal/JOURNEY.md](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/workspace/reports/research-journey-20261019/journal/JOURNEY.md)

# Usable split baseline

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

What repeatable service configuration can serve as a baseline for later controlled tuning?

## Why investigate this?

Once the team had a working disaggregated path, it needed a stable reference before changing backends or load. Two prefill replicas can process independent prompts while a decode worker generates their continuations. Tensor parallel (TP) spreads layer computation across GPUs; expert parallel (EP) distributes the MoE experts. A baseline makes later candidate/control comparisons interpretable.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| H200 role allocation | Earlier topology experiments and recovery paths. | Two TP4 prefill replicas feed one TP8/EP8 decode worker; subsequent full runs and controls use this as the retained split baseline. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 job 22415 | N48: 1,912.30 good output tokens/s. |
| Later controls | Near 1,911 good output tokens/s. |

## What did we learn?

- The configuration provided a usable reference point for matched tuning.
- The close later controls suggest this operating point was reproducible at that stage.

## Decision

Retain it as a matched-tuning baseline, not as a claim of globally optimal topology.

## Limits and remaining questions

- The measurements are from the historical workload and system state.
- The evidence does not exhaustively compare every possible layout.

# Cold-prefill cache candidate

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Does a cold-prefill cache intervention raise H200 goodput enough to offset its latency-tail behavior?

## Why investigate this?

The cold-prefix workload offers little benefit from reusable prefix lookup. The team tested whether removing radix-tree bookkeeping on prefill could improve useful throughput. This changes the cache implementation used by prefill; it does not remove the KV state needed for active requests.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Prefill cache implementation | disable_radix_cache=false; Python RadixCache on both prefill roles. | disable_radix_cache=true; ChunkCache on both prefill roles. |
| Decode cache and workload | Decode ChunkCache; cold-prefix workload, seed 2026. | Unchanged; active-request KV storage remains enabled. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| Candidate peak | 3,048.446289 good output tokens/s; +0.240921% versus control. |
| Tail behavior | p95 TTFT worsened. |

## What did we learn?

- The small score difference was below the 1% promotion threshold.
- A worsened p95 TTFT weakens the case despite a higher peak.

## Decision

Do not promote; keep the existing recipe.

## Limits and remaining questions

- The result applies to this specific cache design and cold workload.
- No claim about warm-cache workloads or other cache strategies.

# Direct H100-derived recipe check on H200

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Do H100-derived decode recipes or FA3 transfer to the H200 incumbent?

## Why investigate this?

A configuration that works on H100 may interact differently with H200 hardware and software. The correct test is direct H200 measurement against a fresh H200 control, keeping same-GPU comparisons intact. FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and the H100-derived recipe are existing options, not presumed upgrades.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| H200 control | Prior incumbent reference. | Fresh H200 control at 3,038.022907 good output tokens/s. |
| Transferred backend | H200 incumbent decode. | FA3 decode and H100-derived recipe tested at N54/N64. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| FA3 on H200 | −1.276% versus fresh control. |
| H100 recipe on H200 | N64: −10.408% versus control. |

## What did we learn?

- Neither tested transfer beat the H200 control.
- The result supports hardware-specific recipes rather than pooled GPU ranking.

## Decision

Retain the H200-specific incumbent and do not port these settings unchanged.

## Limits and remaining questions

- The conclusion applies to the tested FA3/H100 recipe versions and loads.
- It does not show those techniques are universally inferior on H200.

# Equal-TP recovery and preserved losses

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Would a separately scoped equal-TP8 descriptor route make the transfer path reliable at larger request loads?

## Why investigate this?

After the first patch enabled a real request path, this branch tested another parallel layout and descriptor route. The rationale is retrospective from the sequence of topology recovery experiments: a path that works at a small load may still fail eligibility as concurrency rises. The evidence should be used to understand the tested option, not as proof that equal TP itself is intrinsically unsuitable.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel layout/transfer route | Heterogeneous prefill and decode TP widths. | A separately scoped equal-TP8 descriptor route; related partial and timeout attempts were retained. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 job 22809 | 1,507.96 good output tokens/s at N32; 95.38% joint SLA fraction. |
| Larger loads | N40 and N48 attempts did not meet eligibility. |

## What did we learn?

- A scored N32 run was possible, but it did not meet the joint request-quality gate.
- Higher-load failures made this branch unsuitable for promotion under the tested setup.

## Decision

Do not select this branch; retain the failures and continue from the denser split baseline.

- The score is not comparable with other runs at different layouts or loads.
- No evidence isolates TP equality as the cause of SLA failure.

# H100 both-phase HPC-Ops

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Does applying HPC-Ops to prefill as well as decode improve H100 throughput, and where does added load stop helping?

## Why investigate this?

After a repeated decode-only result, the next bounded question was whether the same existing library helped the prompt-processing phase too. Prefill operates on many prompt tokens at once, so its behavior can differ from sequential decode. Subsequent N54/N56 trials examined whether increasing client concurrency yielded additional useful goodput.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| H100 backend coverage | HPC-Ops selected for decode. | HPC-Ops added to prefill while retaining the decode path; load refined with repeats. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| Initial comparison | 2,371.961 versus 2,308.979 control. |
| N54 full runs | 2,430.891 and repeat 2,418.588 good output tokens/s. |
| N56 | No further gain established. |

## What did we learn?

- The all-phase recipe improved the observed H100 operating point in later N54 trials.
- N56 did not justify pushing the load higher.

## Decision

Keep the measured H100 recipe/load as a platform-specific candidate; stop increasing concurrency without useful evidence.

## Limits and remaining questions

- The observations are H100-specific.
- The contribution of prefill HPC-Ops versus interaction with decode/load was not fully isolated.

# H100 HPC-Ops decode

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

On H100, does selecting HPC-Ops for decode improve the full service relative to the existing decode backend?

## Why investigate this?

The earlier H200 result suggested HPC-Ops was worth testing as an existing decode implementation on H100, but hardware transfer was uncertain. Decode repeatedly applies the model to one next token; backend choices can shift time between streaming and first-token behavior. The H100 test therefore needs its own matched control and repeat.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Decode backend on H100 | Existing/automatic decode implementation. | HPC-Ops selected for decode only; treatment repeated against controls. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H100 matched comparison | 2,308.308 versus 2,245.534 good output tokens/s (+2.7955%). |
| Repeat/control | Repeat 2,304.083 remained above fresh control job 221275. |
| Latency tradeoff | ITL improved; TTFT rose. |

## What did we learn?

- The full-service gain repeated in the same H100 context.
- The change shifted latency metrics: higher goodput and better token spacing came with slower first-token time.

## Decision

Retain HPC-Ops decode as a supported H100 option under the tested recipe.

## Limits and remaining questions

- H100-only evidence; do not infer H200 effect.
- This is configuration-level evidence and does not isolate an individual kernel cause.

- The tested chunk sweep did not produce a promoted H100 improvement.

# H100 prefill alternatives lose

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Do alternative H100 prefill chunking or dense FlashInfer attention improve the current H100 recipe?

## Why investigate this?

Once the H100 baseline recipe existed, chunk size and attention implementation were plausible controls on prompt processing. Smaller chunks can change scheduling and memory behavior; FlashInfer is an existing attention implementation. The decision criterion was complete-service performance under matched conditions, not whether a branch passed basic validity checks.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|

|---|---|

| H100 dense FlashInfer | 2,227.031 good output tokens/s, −7.74% versus control. |

## What did we learn?

- Chunk 6144 was effectively a tie/slight loss, not an improvement.
- Dense FlashInfer materially reduced the measured score in this tested recipe.
- Passing run gates only establishes valid execution, not benefit.

- These are specific H100 implementation/settings, not universal library rankings.

# Request-scoped NIXL descriptors

> Retrospective explanation from retained code, tests and run logs. No new experiment was run for this note.

## 1. What problem led to this work?

Workers in historical H200 job **22271** loaded the model and reported ready. A warmup request through both prefill and decode then hit its **360-second deadline**. AIPerf had not started scoring: the team had a service path that was not yet usable, not a low throughput score.

The branch used **TP8/EP2 prefill → TP4/EP4 decode**. This is the historical recovery branch, not the later selected two-TP4-prefill/TP8-decode recipe.

Source: [unpatched warmup log](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/runs/22271/pair-warmup.log), [retained reasoning audit](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/workspace/reports/ai-final-report-20261030/KV_TRANSFER_REASONING_AUDIT.md).

## 2. How did the team find a concrete hypothesis?

The team inspected the SGLang NIXL integration used by the container. When attention tensor-parallel widths differ, this code must map the source KV heads and byte ranges onto the destination ranks.

In the original `_init_hetero_tp_prep_handle`, the code created a slot array across the reserved KV pool and expanded it across K/V layer pointers. That exposed a large piece of **metadata preparation** before useful request execution.

```python
# Extract from the retained original source.
num_slots = self.kv_args.kv_data_lens[0] // src_kv_item_len
slots = np.arange(num_slots, dtype=np.uint64)
```

For the representative source geometry, **2,148,119 slots × 94 layers × K/V = 403,846,372 source entries per rank**. A single request uses only its allocated pages.

A descriptor describes an address, length and device. Preparing descriptors for the whole pool does **not** mean the old code transmitted the whole KV pool. The proposed intervention reduced setup metadata, while preserving the bytes each request needed.

Source: [original source around pool enumeration](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/original-conn.py#L858), [patch metadata and scope](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/metadata.json).

## 3. Why investigate this before bandwidth or scheduling?

- The failure appeared during initial pair warmup, before a scored service run.
- Source inspection identified a specific setup operation that scaled with reserved pool capacity.
- A bounded change could be checked against the original byte ranges on CPU before another distributed run.

This made metadata preparation a practical first experiment. It did not establish that bandwidth, KV layout or scheduling were healthy, or that descriptor construction alone caused the timeout.

## 4. What exactly changed?

| Location | Original implementation | Patched implementation |
|---|---|---|
| `_init_hetero_tp_prep_handle` | Prepare descriptor lists covering reserved pool slots. | Store compact pointer/stride/head geometry in `_ondemand_slice_plans`. |
| `send_kvcache_slice` | Select transfers from prepared pool lists. | Construct source and destination address ranges from this request's page lists. |
| Adjacent ranges | Numerous per-token entries in the pool representation. | Coalesce contiguous runs only when source and destination bytes can safely be represented as whole-token ranges. |
| Partial KV-head slices | Preserve per-token addressing. | Still preserve per-token stride; do not merge over unrelated head bytes. |
| Model and other paths | Original checkpoint, precision, head mapping and notifications. | Retained; equal-TP transfers are outside this patch's scope. |

Source: [reviewable patch](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/nixl-ondemand.patch), [patched preparation](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/conn.py#L776), [patched send path](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/conn.py#L1616).

## 5. Why is the coalescing condition important?

The implementation merges only when the transfer covers a whole source token and a whole destination token:

```python
if length == plan["src_stride"] == plan["dst_stride"]:
    boundary[1:] = (
        (src_tokens[1:] != src_tokens[:-1] + 1)
        | (dst_tokens[1:] != dst_tokens[:-1] + 1)
    )
```

**Illustration, not a measurement:** two required ranges `[0, 100)` and `[100, 200)` can become `[0, 200)`. But ranges `[0, 100)` and `[400, 500)` must remain separate. Merging them would include bytes the request did not ask to transfer. Source and destination must both be contiguous; continuity on just one side is insufficient.

## 6. How was correctness checked before using GPUs?

The CPU harness extracted the actual old and new functions, replaced the NIXL transfer calls with a recording stub, and compared the resulting source/destination byte slices and notifications.

| Coverage | Retained check |
|---|---|
| Attention TP | 2, 4 and 8; heterogeneous directions and relevant ranks. |
| KV heads | 4 and 8. |
| Page size | 1, 4 and 16. |
| Request pages | Contiguous, noncontiguous and single-page patterns. |
| Equivalence cases | **720 passed**. |
| Full-size geometry example | 94 layers, 4,000 contiguous prompt tokens, TP8→TP4: **188 request descriptors**. |

The 188 entries correspond to one coalesced range for each K/V layer in that example. The 403.8-million and 188 counts describe different scopes; they are not an inference speedup ratio.

Source: [CPU test harness](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/test-nixl-ondemand.py), [recorded geometry result](https://github.com/trungdangtapcode/apac-hpc-ai-2026/blob/main/2026-APAC-HPC-AI/qwen-experiments/nixl-ondemand/geometry-test.json).

## 7. What happened on the real serving path?

| Observation | Before: 22271 | Patched: 22294 |
|---|---|---|
| Worker model load | Ready. | Ready. |
| Pair warmup | Deadline expired at 360 seconds. | Both tested P/D routes completed, about 0.68–0.70 seconds/request after readiness. |
| Full benchmark | Not reached; no score. | Full N32 confirmation completed. |
| Good output throughput | No scored result. | **1,422.96 good output tokens/s**. |
| Joint latency pass share | No scored result. | **95.87%**. |
| Scored errors / cancellations | No scored result. | **0 / 0**. |

The team kept the change because the patched branch completed real requests and a full benchmark. The CPU checks established intended range equivalence in tested geometries; the GPU run supplied the separate end-to-end execution evidence.

## 8. What can this result establish?

## Research question

Do phase-specific inference-mode changes improve H200 goodput beyond a no-grad control?

## Why investigate this?

The test checked a narrow runtime change separately in prefill and decode. Inference mode can reduce framework bookkeeping for operations that do not require autograd; applying it to only one phase helps identify whether the change matters in this serving path. - Both measured differences were well below the 1% useful-gain threshold.
- No phase-mode variant justified changing the incumbent.

# Tokenizer, prefill attention and EAGLE losses

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Do tokenizer, prefill-attention, or shallow speculative-decoding changes improve the H200 incumbent?

## Why investigate this?

The team screened several distinct ideas against the current H200 context: dynamic tokenization may reduce client overhead, an alternative attention backend may change prefill computation, and shallow EAGLE3 speculation may reduce sequential decode work. Each mechanism affects a different stage, so results should not be combined into one general backend claim.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Tokenization | Existing tokenizer path. | Dynamic tokenizer variants. |
| Prefill attention | Incumbent attention backend. | FlashInfer prefill. |
| Decode generation | Ordinary decode. | Shallow EAGLE3 draft/verification path. |

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 dynamic tokenizer | +0.192% / +0.270%; not promoted. |
| FlashInfer prefill | −6.385%. |
| Shallow EAGLE3 | −2.080%. |

## What did we learn?

- Small tokenizer differences were below the useful-gain bar.
- FlashInfer prefill and shallow speculation reduced goodput in these tests.

- Percentages apply to the cited matched tests and versions.

# Round-robin prefill routing

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Can assigning new prompts across the prefill replicas more evenly reduce first-token delay?

## Why investigate this?

The workload deliberately disabled prefix reuse. The source review noted a cache-aware prefill policy with an absolute imbalance threshold of 64 while the tested burst was N52. This suggested testing deterministic distribution across the two prefill replicas to reduce the first-burst TTFT tail. It was a routing hypothesis, not proof of a router bug.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Prefill gateway policy | Inherited cache_aware policy; absolute imbalance threshold 64 in the reviewed control. | Set --prefill-policy round_robin; worker, decode and client files unchanged. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 pilot 23325 | 2,402.64 good output tokens/s versus 2,075.11 control. |
| Mean TTFT | 1,437.63 ms to 333.25 ms in the pilot. |

## What did we learn?

- The pilot observed higher goodput and much lower mean time to first token.
- It was a single treatment observation; inter-token latency approached its limit, so request-level tails remained important.

## Decision

Use the routing change as a promising lead and seek controlled follow-up rather than treating the pilot as settled.

## Limits and remaining questions

- Single pilot observation; not an independent replication.
- The exact causal contribution of routing is not established by the score difference.

# Complete paired local answer-quality test

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

On the complete paired MMLU-Pro set, does the accepted candidate retain at least 99% of the stock FP8 reference score?

## Why investigate this?

The pilot was below the local point gate, so the team evaluated the complete 12,032-question set with fixed prompts, settings, parser, and eight paired shards. The question is score retention relative to the stock FP8 reference, not whether the candidate answers every item correctly. Identical evaluation scope makes the local ratio interpretable, while organiser certification remains separate.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Quality evaluation | Small N16 pilot. | Full paired 12,032-question MMLU-Pro evaluation of stock FP8 reference and accepted candidate across eight paired shards. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| Stock FP8 reference | 9,460 / 12,032 correct = 78.623670%. |
| Candidate | 9,452 / 12,032 correct = 78.557181%. |
| Retention | 9,452 / 9,460 = 99.915433%; above the local 99% point gate. |

## What did we learn?

- The candidate scored eight fewer questions correctly than the reference.
- The measured point estimate passes the local ≥99%-of-reference criterion.

## Decision

Record this as a local full-set point-gate pass, not a BTC-certified quality PASS.

## Limits and remaining questions

- This does not establish statistical equivalence on future data.
- It is not organiser certification; acceptance and quality are distinct checks.
- The quality pilot failed the local gate; the full-set result supersedes it for the final local assessment.

# Sparse decode graph experiment

> Source-linked retrospective. Original measurements remain attributed to their platform, load and trial.

## Research question

Can reducing decode graph buckets lower memory use and improve service goodput?

## Why investigate this?

The hypothesis was that fewer captured graph variants might reduce memory pressure. Graph capture prepares reusable GPU execution paths; however, a memory proxy is not itself the competition metric. The full run tests whether the reduced footprint translates into qualifying-request throughput.

## What changed?

| Aspect | Before / control | After / tested setting |
|---|---|---|
| Decode graph batch buckets | Dense list 1–64 (64 captures). | [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 50, 52, 54, 56, 64] (12 captures). Maximum 64 retained. |
| Compilation | torch.compile disabled. | Still disabled; this is a graph-bucket trial, not a compile speedup. |

## What was measured?

| Evidence | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| H200 job 27510 | 3,029.861122 good output tokens/s, −0.370208%. |
| Memory per rank | 1.15 GB to 0.36 GB. |
| Logged capture memory per rank | 1.15 → 0.36 GB; native capture log label, not total sampled VRAM. |
| Logged capture time | 101.46–101.49 → 95.98–96.05 seconds. |

## What did we learn?

- The memory measure fell substantially, but goodput did not improve.
- Lower memory use alone was not sufficient to justify a slower measured service.

## Decision

Close the sparse-graph candidate under the current objective.

## Limits and remaining questions

- Memory figures are the recorded graph-related measure, not total GPU VRAM.
- No evidence that graph memory constrained this deployment.

findings: Chunk 8192 recovered performance relative to 4096 within this transferred branch.
Recovery did not make the recipe competitive with the retained H200 incumbent.
limits: The result is a branch-level comparison, not evidence that chunk 8192 is globally best.
Different controls and recipe settings prohibit combining these values with unrelated series.
preview.question: Can chunk-size refinement recover performance when the H100-derived HPC-Ops prefill runner is used on H200?
preview.rationale: The prior H100 recipe transferred poorly to H200, but the runner and chunk size can interact. Rather than reject every component, this branch held the HPC-Ops prefill runner and changed chunk size, then compared its best point with the incumbent. This isolates the chunk refinement within that transferred recipe, while still requiring a direct incumbent comparison.
